notes.summary: The supplied section follows Ulysses’ obstructed homecoming, Telemachus’ search for his father, the suitors’ consumption of the household and their ambush plot, and Ulysses’ passage from Calypso’s captivity through shipwreck to Phaeacian hospitality. Songs and recollections expose the grief and violence behind heroic fame. Ulysses then identifies himself and recounts the Cicons, Lotus-eaters, and Cyclops. The section ends inside the Cyclops’ cave: Ulysses has prepared an olive-wood weapon, intoxicated the monster, and called himself Noman; the Cyclops promises to eat him last. The planned attack and escape have not occurred within the supplied text.

themes.name: Homecoming and attachment to place
themes.meaning: Home remains the central desire despite captivity, wealth, divine beauty, and offered immortality. Ithaca’s ruggedness strengthens rather than diminishes its emotional value.

evidence.quote: the smoke of his own chimneys.
Nevertheless, I want to get home, and can think of nothing else.
It is a rugged island, but it breeds brave men,

themes.name: Human responsibility and divine interference
themes.meaning: The narrative repeatedly places human folly beside divine causation. These explanations coexist and sometimes differ between speakers.

evidence.quote: they perished through their own sheer folly
how men lay blame upon us gods
Jove saw fit to vex the Argives on their homeward voyage;
my men very foolishly would not obey me,

themes.name: Hospitality tested, upheld, and inverted
themes.meaning: Receiving strangers with food, washing, shelter, and assistance establishes a recurring ethical test. The suitors exploit hospitality; the Cyclops turns the expected guest-gift into a threat of consumption.

evidence.quote: he was vexed that a stranger should be kept waiting for admittance.
show the strangers in that they may have supper;
treat a guest and a suppliant as though he were his own brother.
This is the present that I will make him.

themes.name: The household under siege
themes.meaning: Eating, courtship, and political intimidation become mechanisms for exhausting an estate and threatening its surviving heir. The later ambush makes the danger explicit.

evidence.quote: my house is being disgraced and ruined.
divide up his property amongst us:
I will lie in wait for him in the straits between Ithaca and Samos;

themes.name: Coming of age through speech and action
themes.meaning: Telemachus moves from private brooding to public assembly, independent travel, and questioning elders. Courage remains assisted by Minerva rather than becoming effortless confidence.

evidence.quote: she had given Telemachus courage,
Telemachus dashed his staff to the ground and burst into tears.
I have never yet been used to holding long conversations with people,
Telemachus answered boldly,

themes.name: Inheritance, resemblance, and threatened continuity
themes.meaning: Fatherhood connects bodily resemblance, reputation, property, and political authority. Telemachus’ uncertain knowledge of his father and Penelope’s fear of losing her son make continuity precarious.

evidence.quote: I inherit nothing but dismay.
His hands and feet are just like Ulysses;
trying to exterminate his own race and that of Ulysses.

themes.name: Cunning, concealment, and control of identity
themes.meaning: Disguise and withheld identity allow gods and mortals to act under unequal conditions. Ulysses’ resourcefulness culminates here in preparation and the name Noman, without a completed escape.

evidence.quote: entered the enemy’s city looking like a menial or a beggar,
Minerva shed a thick mist all round him
I answered with a lie;
my name is Noman;

themes.name: Memory, song, and grief
themes.meaning: Songs preserve heroic deeds while reopening private suffering. The section eventually compares Ulysses’ tears to those of a bereaved woman carried into slavery, widening the emotional perspective beyond victorious warriors.

evidence.quote: it breaks my sorrowful heart,
Ulysses drew his purple mantle over his head and covered his face,
carry her off into slavery, to a life of labour and sorrow,
rekindle my own sad memories

themes.name: Forgetting as comfort and danger
themes.meaning: Sleep and Helen’s drug ease sorrow, while lotus consumption extinguishes the desire to return. Relief from painful memory can restore a traveller or interrupt his purpose.

evidence.quote: an herb that banishes all care, sorrow, and ill humour.
made him lose all memories of his sorrows.
those who ate of it left off caring about home,

themes.name: Endurance, bodily vulnerability, and recovery
themes.meaning: Heroic capability survives exhaustion, hunger, torn skin, nakedness, and tears. Shelter, food, clothing, and bathing visibly restore Ulysses before his athletic demonstration.

evidence.quote: the rocks tear the skin from his strong hands,
lay swooning from sheer exhaustion;
ate and drank ravenously,
flew beyond any mark that had been made yet.

themes.name: Craft overcoming superior strength
themes.meaning: Making, binding, weaving, and shaping offer alternatives to brute force. Vulcan’s trap supplies an explicit parallel to Ulysses’ emerging plan against the physically overwhelming Cyclops.

evidence.quote: fitted the timbers together with bolts and rivets.
the weak confound the strong.
charring the end in the fire to make it harder.

themes.name: Marriage, fidelity, and coercion
themes.meaning: Marriage appears as mutual household harmony, political exchange, pressured courtship, divine jealousy, and betrayal. Calypso’s confinement and Alcinous’ voluntary offer create markedly different conditions for remaining abroad.

evidence.quote: he was forced to sleep with her in the cave by night,
man and wife should be of one mind in a house.
no one (heaven forbid) shall keep you here against your own wish,
defiled King Vulcan’s marriage bed,

themes.name: Revenge, warning, and accountability
themes.meaning: Orestes’ revenge repeatedly serves as an example for Telemachus. Ignored warnings recur in Aegisthus’ story, the suitors’ response to omens, and the Cyclops’ rejection of divine protection.

evidence.quote: Mercury told him this in all good will but he would not listen,
Would that heaven might grant me to do like vengeance
birds are always flying about in the sunshine somewhere or other, but they seldom mean anything.
We Cyclopes do not care about Jove

themes.name: Public order and collective failure
themes.meaning: Assemblies distinguish organized civic life from isolated power, but institutions do not guarantee justice. Ithaca’s people remain passive, while Phaeacian collective action supplies an escort.

evidence.quote: you all sit still without even trying to stop such scandalous goings on
man her with two and fifty of our smartest young sailors.
They have no laws nor assemblies of the people,

objects.name: Ithaca: rugged homeland and occupied house
objects.meaning: A forested, uneven island and an endangered domestic estate give homecoming its concrete destination. The house’s threshold, court, cloisters, storeroom, and upper rooms offer distinct staging spaces.

evidence.quote: the country is more fit for goats than horses,
Telemachus’s room was high up in a tower
the lofty and spacious store-room

objects.name: Ogygia: Calypso’s cave and cultivated surroundings
objects.meaning: Luxuriant vegetation, running water, fragrance, and weaving surround a captive who spends his days grieving on the shore. The beautiful setting does not satisfy his desire for home.

evidence.quote: A vine loaded with grapes
four running rills of water
looking out upon the barren ocean with tears in his eyes,

objects.name: Pylos: sacrificial shore and hospitable household
objects.meaning: The shore initially appears as a large organized ritual gathering; Nestor’s house then provides lodging, instruction, and the means for onward travel.

evidence.quote: offer sacrifice of black bulls to Neptune
soft sheepskins that were lying on the sands
benches of white and polished marble

objects.name: Lacedaemon: Menelaus’ glittering palace
objects.meaning: A wedding feast and brilliant imported materials frame grief that wealth cannot repair. Helen’s textile equipment adds a specific domestic focal point.

evidence.quote: the low lying city of Lacedaemon,
the gleam of bronze and gold—of amber,40 ivory, and silver.
I have no pleasure in being lord of all this wealth.

objects.name: Pharos: becalmed island and seal-haunted sea cave
objects.meaning: Menelaus’ embedded story supplies a distinct setting of hunger, stalled ships, a sea cave, and an ambush beneath animal skins.

evidence.quote: the gods becalmed me twenty days
goes to sleep in a great sea cave,
dug four pits for us to lie in,

objects.name: Asteris: double-harboured ambush island
objects.meaning: A small rocky site gives the suitors’ concealed violence a precise location. Their attack remains pending in the supplied section.

evidence.quote: a rocky islet called Asteris,
a harbour on either side of it

objects.name: Scheria: dangerous coast and sheltered river mouth
objects.meaning: Surf-beaten rocks initially deny landing; the river offers an answered prayer and a transition from drowning danger to terrestrial shelter.

evidence.quote: the coast is rocky and surf-beaten,
the mouth of a river,
kissed the bounteous earth.

objects.name: Scheria: washing place, sacred grove, and maritime city
objects.meaning: Domestic work at the stream leads to rescue, then to a grove and a city organized around ships and shipbuilding.

evidence.quote: a high beach of shingle,
a beautiful grove of poplars
a temple of Neptune in the middle of it,

objects.name: Alcinous’ palace and perpetual garden
objects.meaning: Metallic architecture, crafted guardians, torch-bearing figures, woven furnishings, and continuous fruitfulness make the palace a concentrated setting of abundance and skill.

evidence.quote: the cornice was of blue enamel.
gold and silver mastiffs
golden figures of young men with lighted torches in their hands,
The fruits never rot nor fail all the year round,

objects.name: Ismarus and the Cicon shore
objects.meaning: A raid, captured women, shared booty, prolonged feasting, and a retaliatory battle complicate Ulysses’ role as a sufferer by showing him as an aggressor.

evidence.quote: There I sacked the town and put the people to the sword.
They set the battle in array near the ships,

objects.name: Goat island and the Cyclops’ enclosed cave
objects.meaning: An uninhabited fertile island contrasts with a carefully managed dairy cave whose immense doorway stone turns shelter into imprisonment.

evidence.quote: a wooded and fertile island
a great cave overhung with laurels.
His cheese-racks were loaded with cheeses,
he rolled a huge stone to the mouth of the cave

objects.name: Ships, sails, oars, and the constructed raft
objects.meaning: Vessels connect search, trade, rescue, raiding, and ambush. Ulysses’ hand-built raft displays competence yet remains vulnerable; the Phaeacian ships are described as understanding their passengers’ intentions.

evidence.quote: ropes of twisted ox hide.
He also made a mast with a yard arm, and a rudder to steer with.
the raft, which then went to pieces
the ships themselves understand what it is that we are thinking about and want;

objects.name: Clothing, veils, and mantles
objects.meaning: Textiles mark dignity, grief, modesty, recognition, and rescue. Their functions change: Calypso’s clothes impede swimming, Ino’s veil protects, and the Phaeacian clothes reveal a connection to Arete’s household.

evidence.quote: he held his cloak before his face with both hands.
the clothes Calypso had given him weighed him down;
take my veil and put it round your chest;
as the work of herself and of her maids;

objects.name: Looms, distaffs, yarn, and the unfinished pall
objects.meaning: Weaving links domestic labour, cultivated skill, and Penelope’s resistance through delay. Calypso, Helen, Arete, and Phaeacian servants extend the textile imagery across settings.

evidence.quote: a pall for the hero Laertes,
at night she would unpick the stitches again by torchlight.
a distaff charged with violet coloured wool
shooting her golden shuttle through the warp
spinning her purple wool by firelight.

objects.name: Wine, mixing bowls, cups, and travel stores
objects.meaning: Wine sustains travellers, accompanies sacrifice and friendship, enables excess, suppresses grief, and finally becomes an instrument against the Cyclops.

evidence.quote: Let me have twelve jars,
She drugged the wine
of pure silver, except the rim, which is inlaid with gold.
an ivy-wood bowl of black wine
three times did he drain it without thought or heed;

objects.name: Livestock, sacrificial grain, and fire
objects.meaning: Animals appear as wealth, provisions, offerings, and stolen or consumed resources. Similar materials serve radically different moral situations.

evidence.quote: the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion;
the smith gilded the horns of the heifer
wrapped them round in two layers of fat,
some bruised barley into a basket
a drink of neat milk,

objects.name: Water vessels, baths, and anointing oil
objects.meaning: Repeated washing and oiling make hospitality and restored bodily dignity visible. These practices recur from royal banquets to Nausicaa’s improvised assistance.

evidence.quote: a beautiful golden ewer
a silver basin
the little golden cruse of oil,
a tripod full of bath water

objects.name: Birds, divine flight, and omens
objects.meaning: Bird imagery connects revelation, divine travel, and warning. Some appearances are explicit transformations; others are comparisons and should be illustrated accordingly.

evidence.quote: Jove sent two eagles
she flew away in the form of an eagle,
like a cormorant
rising like a sea-gull from the waves,

objects.name: Dawn, stars, clouds, and winds
objects.meaning: Repeated dawns structure departures and renewals. Stars guide navigation, while winds and cloud turn the sea into an arena of divine obstruction and assistance.

evidence.quote: rosy-fingered Dawn,
the Pleiads, on late-setting Bootes, and on the Bear
Winds from East, South, North, and West
she bound the ways of all the winds except one,

objects.name: Olive wood, leaves, and preserved fire
objects.meaning: Olive imagery supports shelter, toolmaking, and planned resistance. The leaf-covered survivor is compared to a hidden ember, suggesting life preserved through exhaustion.

evidence.quote: two shoots of olive that grew from a single stock
hides a brand as fire-seed in the ashes
a beautiful olive-wood handle
it was of green olive wood,

objects.name: Lyres and the wooden horse
objects.meaning: The lyre mediates public entertainment and painful recollection. The wooden horse is explicitly present in remembered and sung events, linking craftsmanship, concealment, and the destruction of Troy.

evidence.quote: a lyre to Phemius,
He hung the lyre for him on a peg over his head,
the wooden horse which Epeus made with the assistance of Minerva,
issued from the horse, and sacked the town,

objects.name: Discs, dancing balls, and sporting ground
objects.meaning: Games test reputation and provoke Ulysses’ renewed assertion of strength. Ball play also initiates his encounter with Nausicaa, creating a recurring connection between leisure and recognition.

evidence.quote: threw a ball at one of the maids,
a disc, larger, more massive and much heavier
a red ball which Polybus had made for them,

objects.name: Bonds, knots, nets, and enclosure
objects.meaning: Binding can protect possessions, restrain companions, expose adultery, or trap vulnerable bodies. The motif links literal devices with similes of threatened capture.

evidence.quote: chains like cobwebs;
Like a lioness caught in the toils
a bond that Circe had taught him.
made them fast under the benches.

objects.name: Proteus’ transformations and seal-skin disguise
objects.meaning: A sequence of changing forms provides an explicitly narrated visual subject in Menelaus’ recollection. The enacted transformations differ slightly from Idothea’s advance description.

evidence.quote: threw a seal skin over each of us.
a lion with a great mane;
a dragon, a leopard, a wild boar;
he was running water, and then again directly he was a tree,

objects.name: Lotus flower-food
objects.meaning: The lotus provides a small, potent object whose pleasurable consumption dissolves the purpose of the voyage. Its botanical identity is unspecified.

evidence.quote: a food that comes from a kind of flower.
without thinking further of their return;

objects.name: The Cyclops’ olive-wood weapon and promised guest-gift
objects.meaning: The final scene juxtaposes hidden preparation, intoxication, and verbal deception with the monster’s murderous parody of generosity. The weapon is prepared but not yet used.

evidence.quote: cut off about six feet of it;
I hid it under dung,
bore it into the monster’s eye while he was asleep.
will keep Noman for the last.

relationships.name: Minerva and Ulysses’ family
relationships.meaning: Minerva advocates for Ulysses, mentors Telemachus through disguises, and comforts Penelope through a vision. Her help often operates without open recognition.

evidence.quote: it is for Ulysses that my heart bleeds,
in the likeness and with the voice of Mentor.
it is she who has compassion upon you,
she would not show herself to him openly,

relationships.name: Neptune, Polyphemus, and Ulysses
relationships.meaning: Neptune’s hostility is explicitly connected to his son’s injured eye. The later retrospective cave narrative begins to supply the circumstances behind that hostility.

evidence.quote: Polyphemus is son to Neptune
having blinded an eye of Polyphemus king of the Cyclopes.
he shall have plenty of hardship yet

relationships.name: Calypso and Ulysses
relationships.meaning: Care, desire, captivity, and coercion coexist. Calypso offers immortality, obeys the divine release order, and helps build and provision the departure, while Ulysses continues to choose home.

evidence.quote: had set my heart on making him immortal,
it was she, not he, that would have it so.
I mean you no sort of harm,
I want to get home,

relationships.name: Penelope, Ulysses, and Telemachus
relationships.meaning: The absent husband and endangered son concentrate Penelope’s grief. Telemachus asserts authority over her speech yet refuses to expel her from the household.

evidence.quote: for speech is man’s matter,
how can I drive the mother who bore me from my father’s house?
I am even more anxious about him than about my husband;

relationships.name: The suitors and the household
relationships.meaning: The suitors blame Penelope’s delaying tactics, deny Telemachus’ effective authority, consume his resources, and ultimately organize his murder.

evidence.quote: It is your mother’s fault not ours,
so long shall we go on eating up your estate;
intent on murdering Telemachus.

relationships.name: Euryclea and Telemachus’ family
relationships.meaning: Euryclea’s purchased status coexists with long-standing care, household responsibility, and protective affection. Her oath temporarily places loyalty to Telemachus in tension with informing Penelope.

evidence.quote: Laertes had bought her with his own money
she had nursed him when he was a baby.
he made me take my solemn oath

relationships.name: Nestor, Menelaus, Pisistratus, and Telemachus
relationships.meaning: Friendship with Ulysses extends into hospitality and guidance for his son. Pisistratus becomes an escort and sympathetic peer; the elders’ knowledge remains incomplete.

evidence.quote: He and I never had any kind of difference
the reports that have reached me
My father, Nestor, sent me to escort him hither,
the son of a very dear friend,

relationships.name: Agamemnon, Clytemnestra, Aegisthus, and Orestes
relationships.meaning: The betrayed returning ruler and avenging son form a repeated cautionary parallel to Ithaca. The supplied accounts describe seduction, murder, revenge, and funeral rites without fully narrating every death.

evidence.quote: cajoled Agamemnon’s wife Clytemnestra with incessant flattery.
killed him when the banquet was over
killed the murderer of his father.

relationships.name: Helen, Menelaus, and Ulysses’ remembered exploits
relationships.meaning: Helen describes recognizing and protecting Ulysses in Troy; Menelaus recalls her testing the men hidden in the horse by imitating their wives. Together these recollections complicate her relation to the opposing sides.

evidence.quote: I alone recognised him
a solemn oath not to betray him
mimicked all our wives

relationships.name: Nausicaa and Ulysses
relationships.meaning: A frightened encounter becomes material rescue, admiration, and practical guidance. Nausicaa manages the danger of public gossip; Ulysses later thanks her and protects her from her father’s criticism.

evidence.quote: the daughter of Alcinous stood firm,
I am afraid of the gossip and scandal
Pray do not scold her,
for it was you who saved me.

relationships.name: Arete, Alcinous, and the foreign suppliant
relationships.meaning: Arete’s respected position makes her goodwill central to Ulysses’ reception. Alcinous provides public support, gifts, and a voluntary escort, then asks for identity and the cause of grief.

evidence.quote: respected beyond measure
he laid his hands upon the knees of the queen,
I will attend tomorrow to the matter of your escort.
tell me the name

relationships.name: Bards, listeners, and attentive hosts
relationships.meaning: Phemius is compelled to perform, while Demodocus is honoured as a gifted singer. Alcinous notices the pain that entertaining songs cause his guest and intervenes.

evidence.quote: whom they compelled perforce to sing to them.
she had robbed him of his eyesight.
for all the pain his lays may cause me
let Demodocus cease his song,

relationships.name: Vulcan, Venus, Mars, and Neptune
relationships.meaning: The embedded song turns marital betrayal into capture, public humiliation, and negotiated compensation. Neptune’s guarantee secures release.

evidence.quote: caught in the toils which cunning Vulcan had spread for them,
Mars will be cast in heavy damages.
I will pay you myself.

relationships.name: Idothea, Proteus, and Menelaus
relationships.meaning: A divine daughter assists a mortal in trapping her father to obtain knowledge. The encounter links disguise and endurance to information about both homecoming and absent companions.

evidence.quote: she meant playing a trick upon her father.
we stuck to him and never lost hold,
Ulysses who dwells in Ithaca.

relationships.name: Ulysses and his crew
relationships.meaning: Leadership involves rescue, discipline, shared loss, and fallible decisions. The Cicon episode shows disobedient men, while the cave episode shows Ulysses rejecting their safer proposal.

evidence.quote: we lost half a dozen men from every ship
though they wept bitterly I forced them back to the ships
It would have been indeed better if we had done so but I would not listen to them,

relationships.name: Ulysses, his companions, and the Cyclops
relationships.meaning: A request for protected hospitality meets divine defiance and cannibalism. Ulysses restrains immediate violence because the doorway stone prevents escape, then develops a coordinated deception. The final promise to eat Noman last leaves the relationship unresolved.

evidence.quote: we are your suppliants,
we should never be able to shift the stone
The lot fell upon the very four whom I should have chosen, and I myself made five.
I will eat all Noman’s comrades before Noman himself,

uncertainties: This analysis uses only the supplied prose translation. Footnote numbers and bracketed passages are present, but their explanatory notes are unavailable.

The section ends at p412. Although p49 already mentions Polyphemus’ blinded eye, the retrospective cave narrative has not yet enacted the attack or escape; neither should be presented as the closing scene.
The suitors’ ambush is established at Asteris in p235, but its outcome is not narrated here. Jove’s assurances in p240 are divine statements about what will happen.
Sparta and Lacedaemon name the destination in this translation; detailed modern geographical identifications, including Ithaca’s orientation in p389, cannot be established from the extract alone.
Mentes’ trading voyage in p57 and Mentor’s proposed debt-collection journey in p143 are statements made within Minerva’s disguises, not independently established mortal journeys.

Descriptions supplied by Nestor, Helen, Menelaus, Proteus, and Ulysses are embedded accounts. Their differing explanations of disaster or release should retain their speakers rather than be flattened into a single causal account.
The lotus species and Helen’s grief-banishing herb are unidentified. No modern plant or drug identification is supported.
Idothea predicts fire and water transformations in p189; Menelaus’ enacted list in p192 includes animals, running water, and a tree, but does not explicitly include fire.

Bird and animal comparisons are not always literal transformations. Mercury’s cormorant comparison, Ulysses’ lion comparison, Penelope’s lioness comparison, and the bereaved-woman comparison require this distinction.
Nausicaa’s imminent marriage is asserted by Minerva’s dream-disguise. No specific fiancé or completed marriage is established.
Arete is named only after Nausicaa initially describes her mother. The genealogy in p310–p311 makes her Alcinous’ niece as well as wife; no additional family details should be supplied.
The text mentions funeral rites for Clytemnestra in p138 but does not explicitly narrate who killed her.
The olive shoots and hidden fire-seed in p274 support a visual association with preserved life; that symbolic meaning is interpretive rather than an explicit explanation by the narrator.
Calypso’s and Ulysses’ accounts stress different aspects of their relationship. The explicit coercion in p249 should remain visible alongside later descriptions of care.
Ulysses remains unnamed to the Phaeacians until p389, despite the narrator naming him throughout. Earlier recognition should not be invented.

notes.summary: The section follows Ulysses from the blinding of Polyphemus through failed homeward voyages, Circe’s enchantments, consultation of the dead, the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, and the destruction of his crew after they kill the sun-god’s cattle. He reaches Ithaca through Phaeacian hospitality, returns under Minerva’s disguise, reunites secretly with Telemachus, and tests loyalties while enduring abuse. The ending brings Argos’s recognition and death, Antinous’s assault with a footstool, and Penelope’s request to question the unknown beggar about her husband. Strong visual material includes concealed bodies, bound winds, animal transformations, blood-fed ghosts, memorial oars, predatory birds, mist, thresholds, humble meals, and the contrast between lavish abundance and denied hospitality.

themes.name: Cunning, concealment, and unstable identity
themes.meaning: Cleverness saves lives through false names, concealment, and disguise, but also makes recognition and trust difficult.

evidence.quote: Noman is killing me by fraud;
There was to be a man under the middle sheep,
made up a lying story in the instinctive wiliness of his heart.
At one moment she makes me like a beggar, and the next I am a young man with good clothes on my back;

themes.name: Pride, provocation, and restraint
themes.meaning: Ulysses’s insistence on declaring himself exposes the survivors to revenge; his later endurance of humiliation serves a concealed plan.

evidence.quote: say it was the valiant warrior Ulysses, son of Laertes, who lives in Ithaca.
In one thing only did I disobey Circe’s strict instructions—I put on my armour.
he resolved, however, to endure it and keep himself in check,
he shook his head in silence as he brooded on his revenge.

themes.name: Hospitality as an ethical test
themes.meaning: Guests and suppliants meet protection, generosity, manipulation, cannibalism, or assault. The final request from Penelope continues the testing of the household through its treatment of a stranger.

evidence.quote: You wretch, eat up your visitors in your own house?
for all strangers and beggars are from Jove.
One should treat a guest well as long as he is in the house and speed him when he wants to leave it.
you cannot find it in you to give him even a piece of bread.
I want to see him and ask him some questions.

themes.name: Hunger, feasting, and predation
themes.meaning: Food sustains fellowship but also becomes a trap, a violation of sacred limits, and a means of consuming another household’s wealth. Humans repeatedly become prey.

evidence.quote: the Laestrygonians speared them like fishes and took them home to eat them.
she drugged it with wicked poisons to make them forget their homes,
All deaths are bad enough but there is none so bad as famine.
a man cannot hide away the cravings of a hungry belly;
waste his estate by force, without fear or stint.

themes.name: Homecoming delayed and endangered
themes.meaning: Home appears within reach and repeatedly recedes. Even arrival does not immediately bring recognition, security, or reunion with Penelope.

evidence.quote: our native land showed on the horizon.
away from our own country.
He had been so long away that he did not know it again;
I should have come to much the same bad end in my own house as Agamemnon did,

themes.name: Leadership, dissent, and responsibility
themes.meaning: The crew depends on Ulysses while resisting his decisions. He sometimes shares knowledge, sometimes conceals danger, and faces criticism from both Eurylochus and Telemachus.

evidence.quote: It was all through his sheer folly that those men lost their lives.
whether we live or die we may do so with our eyes open.
I said nothing about the awful monster Scylla,
You force me to yield, for you are many against one,
I do not think, however, the plan you propose will turn out well for either of us.

themes.name: Sleep, intoxication, and vulnerability
themes.meaning: Sleep and drink expose bodies and plans to danger, from Polyphemus’s blinding to opened winds, forbidden slaughter, and Elpenor’s fall. Sleep also permits a peaceful return and relief from grief.

evidence.quote: a deep sleep took hold upon him.
they, and cruel sleep, have ruined me.
he tumbled right off the roof and broke his neck,
the sleep into which you have sent me;
a deep, sweet, and almost deathlike slumber.
Minerva shed sleep over her eyes.

themes.name: Divine protection, punishment, and uncertain favour
themes.meaning: Gods guide, disguise, and rescue, yet also withhold help or punish. Human generosity does not guarantee safety from divine anger.

evidence.quote: But he heeded not my sacrifice,
him whom heaven hates will I in no wise help.
I will shiver their ship into little pieces with a bolt of white lightning
turned it into stone,
help you to hide the treasure

themes.name: Mortality, grief, and the limits of heroic glory
themes.meaning: The dead retain sorrows, attachments, and disputes. Achilles rejects prestige in death, while Anticlea’s untouchable form makes loss physically visible.

evidence.quote: I would rather be a paid servant in a poor man’s house and be above ground than king of kings among the dead.
Thrice I sprang towards her and tried to clasp her in my arms,
the soul flits away as though it were a dream.
He would not answer, but turned away to Erebus

themes.name: Burial, remembrance, and obligations to companions
themes.meaning: Elpenor’s unburied body interrupts the search for knowledge. His requested memorial is later completed, turning a working oar into a marker of remembrance.

evidence.quote: We had left his body unwaked and unburied in Circe’s house,
plant over my grave the oar I used to row with
at the top of the cairn we fixed the oar

themes.name: Storytelling, credibility, and withheld knowledge
themes.meaning: Stories earn gifts and sympathy, convey memories, and conceal identity. Eumaeus distinguishes compassionate hospitality from belief in a traveller’s claims.

evidence.quote: as though you were a practiced bard;
it is not right to talk when one does not know.
do not try to flatter me in this way with vain hopes.
telling one another stories about our misfortunes;
he may have seen or heard something of my unhappy husband.

themes.name: Enchantment, attraction, and bodily transformation
themes.meaning: Beautiful song and luxurious interiors conceal danger. Magical changes alter outward form while leaving consciousness or identity intact.

evidence.quote: singing most beautifully as she worked at her loom,
but their senses were the same as before, and they remembered everything.

uncertainties: Use only the supplied prose for visual facts. Footnote numbers and square-bracketed passages are present, but their editorial explanations are not supplied.

Paragraphs p632–p639 and p797–p798 belong to Ulysses’s assumed Cretan identity and should not be illustrated as verified events in his actual biography. Paragraph p606 is explicitly introduced as a lying story.
Circe’s warnings and Teiresias’s prophecies describe future or conditional events. The inland oar ritual, later death, and completed revenge do not occur within this section.
The Sirens are two singers in this version, but the supplied text gives no anatomical description. Bird-bodied or fish-tailed forms would be imported imagery.
The feared Gorgon head in p538 is not actually seen or sent. Theseus and Pirithous are desired encounters, not witnessed figures.

Circe’s wolves and lions are described as bewitched creatures; their original identities are not established. Eurylochus’s claim that the crew will become guard animals is his warning, not a confirmed event.
Neptune turns the Phaeacian ship into stone, but burial of the city under a mountain remains threatened; its fulfilment is not narrated here.
The text’s bracketed reference to the '[Wandering] rocks' in p561 creates uncertainty about how precisely to identify these with the separately described Wanderers and the Scylla–Charybdis passage.
Statements about women, enslaved people, and foreign traders are voiced by particular narrators or characters and should not be treated as independently established general truths.
Minerva claims continuing protection, while Ulysses reports not seeing her during his voyage; preserve this difference in their accounts.
The section ends with Penelope requesting the stranger’s attendance. Their interview, her recognition of Ulysses, and the revenge itself are not yet narrated.

notes.summary: The section follows Ulysses from his concealment as a beggar in his own house through tests of hospitality, private recognitions, the bow contest, the killing of the suitors and punishment of servants, and reunion with Penelope and Laertes. It then follows the suitors into Hades and their grieving relatives into renewed conflict. The ending arrests the cycle of revenge: Laertes kills Eupeithes, Minerva stops the fighting, Jove sends a thunderbolt, and Ulysses obeys before Minerva establishes peace. Strong visual material comes from household thresholds, firelight, concealed weapons, woven work, bodily scars, the inherited bow, the rooted marriage bed, cultivated trees, animal comparisons, and the final dropping of weapons.

uncertainties: Ulysses’s accounts as Aethon and Eperitus are concealment narratives. Their claimed ancestry, hospitality, presents, and travel details should not be treated as independently established events.
Amphimedon’s underworld account attributes a destructive intention and coordination to Penelope that differ from the earlier narration. His account is a participant’s perspective.

Theoclymenus’s darkness, ghosts, and blood-dripping architecture belong to prophetic vision; Penelope’s eagle and geese belong to a dream. Animal comparisons elsewhere are similes, not literal transformations, except where divine transformation is expressly narrated.
The description of thunder in p912 includes both clouds in the narration and a clear sky in the miller-woman’s speech. A precise sky depiction would require choosing between those descriptions.
The twelve axes are explicitly pierced through their handle-holes in p982, but their exact construction and arrangement are not fully specified.

Claims about the women’s sexual conduct vary: p990 says the suitors forced them, while other passages describe love, misconduct, or secret relations. Individual consent and culpability cannot be established uniformly.
Euryclea says the twelve women showed no disrespect to Telemachus in p1029; Telemachus accuses them of insolence to him in p1032. Preserve this discrepancy.
Leiodes is described as opposing the suitors’ evil deeds in p953 and repeats that claim in p1017. Ulysses’s accusation about his prayers in p1018 is an inference, not separately verified.
Eurynome covers Ulysses with a cloak in p905, whereas Euryclea claims that action in p915. Euryclea’s description of restraining her disclosure in p1047 also differs from the action narrated in p893.
The oar journey, sacrifices to Neptune, and peaceful old age are reported prophecy. They do not occur within this section.
The final covenant is established, but its precise ritual and the long-term effects of the gods’ proposed forgetting are not narrated.
Chapter headings and embedded footnote numbers belong to the supplied text, but absent footnotes provide no additional evidence. No external adaptation or cover imagery has been used.
